title: Hamas Agrees to Disarm, Russian Missile Strikes Poland, Saudi-Led Coalition Forms to Secure Red Sea
subhead: A landmark Hamas disarmament agreement and a Russian missile crash in NATO-member Poland reshaped the day, while 14 nations joined a Saudi-led maritime alliance and drought forced Central Europe's nuclear plants offline.

sections.heading: Hamas Agrees to Disarm Under Trump's Board of Peace Plan
sections.body:
A senior Hamas official told the BBC that the group has agreed to the Board of Peace's plan for complete disarmament in Gaza, with an official statement expected soon. US President Donald Trump announced the deal on Truth Social, calling it 'a major milestone in the implementation of the Trump 20-Point Plan' and saying Israeli forces would withdraw from Gaza as disarmament proceeds. An International Stabilization Force would work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for security, Trump said.

However, the agreement faces immediate headwinds. An Israeli government statement said the disarmament proposal did not meet Jerusalem's demands, and Israeli media reported that Israel was opposed to the terms being discussed. Hamas previously rejected a disarmament plan in April, and the group's new leader Khalil al-Hayya only recently took over after Yahya Sinwar was killed by Israel in October 2024. Cairo will host a mediator meeting on the second phase of the ceasefire plan, according to AFP. More than 73,290 people have been killed in Gaza since the war began, including 21,280 children, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry.
sections.whyItMatters: If implemented, this would be the first time Hamas agrees to disarm since taking control of Gaza in 2007 — but Israel's rejection signals the deal may stall before it starts.

sections.heading: Russian Missile Crashes in Poland, Violating NATO Airspace
sections.body:
A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in a field near the village of Tarnawa Kolonia in eastern Poland, leaving a 10-metre crater just 92km from the Ukrainian border. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the object was 'in all probability' a Russian cruise missile and confirmed it was armed. The incident occurred during a massive Russian overnight attack on Ukraine that involved more than 70 missiles and 280 drones.

In Ukraine, at least eight people were killed, including five members of the Voronov family — parents Artem and Olena and three of their children — in a village near Kryvyi Rih. Zelensky described it as a 'horrific crime' and reiterated his call for Patriot missile systems. Tusk, who had met Zelensky in Lublin the previous evening, said Poland had been prepared to shoot the missile down if it had continued its flight path. NATO said it was in close contact with Polish authorities, and NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Gen Alexus Grynkewich said the alliance would 'continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory.'
sections.whyItMatters: An armed Russian missile landing deep in NATO territory — not for the first time — raises the stakes for Article 5 considerations every time Russia strikes western Ukraine.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Announces 14-Nation Maritime Alliance for Red Sea
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia announced the creation of the Multinational Maritime Defense Alliance, with 14 nations signing on to safeguard navigation through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The Saudi Defence Ministry said 43 of 51 invited countries participated in the founding meeting, including an EU delegation. Signatories include Turkiye, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Egypt, Pakistan, Djibouti, Somalia, Bangladesh, Yemen, Sudan and the Comoros. Notably absent are the UAE and Oman.

The alliance is framed as purely defensive and comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi-linked vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb have escalated, with the group imposing a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia last week. The virtual closure of the Strait of Hormuz has already diverted significant oil traffic to the Red Sea route, making Bab al-Mandeb a critical chokepoint — only 29km wide at its narrowest — handling 10-12 percent of global maritime trade. It remains unclear what ships or aircraft each country will contribute, and how the alliance will differ from the EU's existing Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea.
sections.whyItMatters: With Hormuz closed, the Red Sea is the only remaining corridor for Gulf oil exports — and the Houthis are targeting it. This coalition is Riyadh's answer, but without UAE and Oman, its regional credibility is incomplete.

sections.heading: US Cyber Agency Warns of Water System Attacks Targeting Minnesota
sections.body:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a warning about a significant increase in hackers targeting water and wastewater systems, after more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota were hit by a 'coordinated cyberattack' on 26-27 July. Attackers targeted programmable logic controllers (PLCs) — the automated computers that control water systems — changing passwords to lock out operators. Boil water notices were issued in affected areas and some systems had to be operated manually.

US investigators are examining whether Iran is behind the attacks, according to multiple media reports, including the New York Times. CISA had already issued guidance in April warning about Iranian-affiliated hackers targeting internet-connected operational devices made by Rockwell Automation, and updated its advisory this month to include devices from other manufacturers. While no water supplies were rendered unsafe, the attack demonstrates the vulnerability of the US's 152,000 public drinking water systems. The incident comes amid resumed US-Iran hostilities after a June ceasefire understanding collapsed.
sections.whyItMatters: A state-attributed cyberattack on American drinking water infrastructure would be a serious escalation in the US-Iran conflict — moving from military exchanges in the Gulf to direct attacks on civilian systems at home.

sections.heading: Danube Drought Forces Nuclear Plant Shutdowns Across Central Europe
sections.body:
Hungary's only nuclear power plant, the Soviet-era Paks facility, will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time because record-low Danube water levels mean its cooling system suction nozzles cannot reach the water. Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned that Hungary's energy supply could become 'critical' from Monday, with temperatures forecast to hover around 37°C for a week. He asked citizens to limit high-energy activities between 17:00 and 22:00 and said rotational blackouts were possible.

Neighbouring Romania has already shut down one of two reactors at its Cernavoda plant, which provides about 20 percent of the country's power, and may close the second. The Danube has fallen to its lowest levels in 30 years across multiple countries, with river flow at the Romanian border down to 1,600 cubic metres per second — less than a third of the July average of 4,700. Shipping has ground to a halt in Bulgaria, and a Viking river cruise ship ran aground near Vidin. Serbian hydrologists say the Danube is at 50-60 year lows, with no improvement expected until mid-September.
sections.whyItMatters: Climate-driven drought is now disabling nuclear power plants that supply baseline electricity to millions — a cascading infrastructure crisis hitting energy, transport and water systems simultaneously.

sections.heading: US GDP Growth Slows to 1.5% as Tariffs and Oil Prices Bite
sections.body:
US GDP grew at just 1.5 percent in the second quarter of 2026, a sharp decline from 2.1 percent in Q1, according to Bureau of Economic Analysis data released on Thursday. The slowdown was driven by a widening trade deficit — exports fell 3.2 percent to $317.7bn while imports rose 3.3 percent to $395.3bn — and volatile petrol prices that hit $4.48 per gallon in May before temporarily easing. Petrol prices have since climbed back above $4.

Tufts professor Michael Klein called it 'a classic supply shock' from the combination of tariffs and oil price spikes. Consumer confidence fell for the third straight month in July, and Bank of America noted that discretionary spending only surged when petrol prices temporarily dipped in June — a K-shaped pattern where high-income earners keep spending while lower-income consumers pull back. The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on 29 July, citing 'elevated' inflation. Meanwhile, countries are actively reducing dependence on the US: Canada has struck new trade deals with China and Saudi Arabia as Trump's tariff policies reshape global trade relationships.
sections.whyItMatters: The US economy is caught between war-driven energy costs and self-imposed trade barriers — a supply shock that no amount of consumer confidence can spend its way out of.

bottomLine: Three stories stand out for what they signal about the shape of conflicts to come. Hamas's agreement to disarm — if it holds — would be the most consequential development in Gaza since the war began, but Israel's rejection makes implementation uncertain at best. The Russian missile in Poland is a reminder that the Ukraine war's spillover risk to NATO is not theoretical; it happens regularly and could escalate at any moment. And the Saudi-led maritime coalition, while still vague on commitments, shows how the closure of Hormuz is forcing regional powers to build new security architecture around the Red Sea — a route that is itself under Houthi attack. Away from the wars, the Danube drought shutting down nuclear plants is a climate-driven infrastructure crisis with no quick fix, and the Minnesota water-system cyberattack raises the question of whether the US-Iran conflict has reached into American civilian infrastructure. US GDP slowing to 1.5% captures the economic toll of all of this at once: tariffs, oil shocks, and trade partners diversifying away.
